1:
Henry opens on the fact that Joshua had already taken what he thought was his last farewell, and that God, in lengthening his days, plainly had further service for him. Gill agrees this is a second gathering of the same representatives, and reports Abarbinel's view that Joshua recalled them because they had answered him nothing before. Wesley finds two ends in the choice of Shechem, the burial of Joseph's bones and the renewing of the covenant, and Henry adds the older associations, that Abraham settled there on first entering Canaan and that Ebal and Gerizim stood close by.

The difficulty is that they presented themselves before God, and Clarke presses it, since that phrase should mean the tabernacle, and the tabernacle was then at Shiloh. He reports the Septuagint reading of Shiloh here, canvasses Shuckford and Mede, and settles the matter by noting that an aged Joshua might assemble the elders where he found convenient and have the ark brought to them. Calvin reaches the same result independently, that the ark was conveyed there not to change its place but that the people might stand before God's earthly tribunal, and Henry reads the sanctuary named later in the chapter as its presence.

Keil and Delitzsch set out the shape of the address, that it recalls every proof of mercy from Abraham's call onward and only then demands the renunciation of idols. Its first stroke is that the fathers beyond the River served other gods, and Clarke and Wesley alike take Abraham to have been no less an idolater than Terah, Clarke identifying the flood as the Euphrates and Ellicott simply as the river. Calvin makes this the hinge of the speech, that Joshua leads them back to an origin where their fathers differed in nothing from their countrymen, so that nothing in Abraham could diminish the grace bestowed. He dismisses the Jewish story that Abraham fled Chaldea for refusing to worship fire, since the text exempts him no more than Terah, and Wesley draws the practical point that the verse forestalls boasting in worthy ancestors.

Gill reads the taking as an apprehending by grace that called and converted him, and Henry, calling him a brand snatched from the burning, makes his justification the apostle's instance of God justifying the ungodly. Calvin notes the seeming contradiction that God multiplied Abraham's seed yet gave him only Isaac, and answers that one alone held the place of lawful heir, as one twin was retained and the other passed over. Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley agree that Esau's possession in Seir left Canaan entire for Jacob, and Keil and Delitzsch add that Joshua assumes the patriarchal history and hurries on to Egypt, tracing the summary through Moses and Aaron and the smiting of both land and people.

Henry notices that the same waters were Israel's guard and Egypt's grave, and that although Exodus records their murmuring it is their crying that is remembered here. He presses the verb used of the wilderness years, that they are said not to wander but to dwell there, as securely as in a walled city, while Wesley reckons that many elders present had seen the plagues themselves. On Balak the sources divide over what his warring amounted to, Clarke observing that no Moabite attack is recorded and taking it for Balaam's curses and the wiles of Midian, Wesley for crafty counsel rather than open force, Ellicott for the sending after Balaam as itself an act of hostility. For the hornets Ellicott sees no reason to read the word other than literally, Henry recalls that they first appeared against Sihon and Og, and Calvin makes them a sharper miracle than any rout, since men who win easily still credit their own valour, but no one can claim a victory won by hornets.
14:
Gill takes the exhortation to fear the Lord as grounded in what precedes, since nothing so moves a reverential affection as a sense of goodness. Clarke divides the charge into four, to reverence him as sole object of worship, to obey his commands, to engage the whole heart, and to keep to his word. Ellicott adds only that the Lord here stands throughout for Jehovah, the covenant God of Israel.

What follows astonishes Clarke, that after all they had seen there should still be idols among them, a thing he finds confirmed later in the chapter and by Amos and by Stephen. He catalogues the three sorts named, the Chaldean worship of fire and the sun, the Egyptian of Apis and Anubis and serpents, and the Canaanite of Baal-peor and Astarte, and suspects the plea was that symbols better represented the divine nature, a defence still made for image-worshipping Christians. Wesley infers that Joshua had purged the public idolatry but some kept it privately, and explains why the older gods were the greater danger, since Canaan's had lately been disgraced by failing to save their worshippers while the others came recommended by antiquity.

The offer of a choice troubles Calvin most of all, since on its face Joshua loosens the reins and gives licence to revolt, and worse still tells them they cannot serve the Lord. He answers that Joshua speaks by the Spirit to draw out their real feelings, since men under God's authority profess zeal readily and build without a foundation, distrusting neither their weakness nor the difficulty of binding themselves wholly. Wesley denies flatly that any liberty was given, since neither Joshua nor they could be released from the law of Moses, and reads the words as an insinuation framed so that a man in his right wits must choose God. Keil and Delitzsch ground the same point in the nature of worship, that it must spring from the heart and cannot be forced by command, and Clarke adds that service which is not voluntary can only be hypocrisy.

Henry works the scene as an election, Jehovah on one side and on the other the gods of their fathers, which recommend themselves to those fond of antiquity, and of their neighbours, which appeal to those fond of good fellowship. He notes that Elijah afterwards referred the same controversy to his hearers' consciences, and holds that religion has reason enough on its side to be safely left to any man who thinks freely. Both Henry and Wesley dwell on Joshua's own declaration, Henry drawing out that he would not set his house to work he would not touch himself, and that we must bring as many as we can where we cannot bring as many as we would. Ellicott turns instead to a curiosity of the record, that no descendant of the conqueror is named and his line closes with him, reading that silence as an analogy with the greater Joshua whose house is all the faithful.

Keil and Delitzsch hear in the answer an echo of the words attached to the first commandment, and take the recital of the signs as assent to all Joshua had rehearsed. Calvin finds the option thereby justified, since they neither swore in another's words nor submitted to dictation, and a covenant is confirmed when a people lay the law upon themselves. Clarke allows they were sincere then, having served the Lord all Joshua's days, and quotes Trapp on how readily a multitude turns with the stream, Rome being pagan, Christian, Arian, apostate and Christian again within one lifetime. Ellicott alone is unimpressed, judging that their horror at apostasy betrayed how little they had understood, and that Joshua's reply shows they had missed his argument.
19:
The declaration that they cannot serve the Lord is the hardest saying in the chapter, and Clarke reports that some critics would emend a single letter to make it read that they shall not cease to serve him. He calls the conjecture ingenious but abandons it, since not one manuscript in the collections of Kennicott and De Rossi supports it, and takes the received text to mean that they cannot serve God while keeping the gods of their fathers. Wesley reads it as a moral rather than an absolute impossibility, alleged not to discourage them but to make them more considerate in binding themselves, since Joshua foresaw that after his death they would find the service burdensome. Calvin agrees the words seem calculated to crush their alert zeal, and answers that the harsh obtestation was needed to rouse a sluggish people, arguing absolutely from the nature of God while aiming at their untamed obstinacy.

Ellicott alone locates the difficulty in Israel's actual practice, that Jehovah will not consent to be served as one God among many, which is precisely what they were doing and continued to do, with rare intervals, until the captivity expelled literal idolatry for good. On his reading they always kept Jehovah as the national deity but never left off recognising the gods of other nations, whom they feared and thought it prudent to propitiate, so Joshua's argument was exactly what those times required. Wesley notes that the Hebrew has holy Gods in the plural and reads the warning about forgiveness narrowly, that a people who own themselves his servants will not be let off as other nations are. Calvin restricts it further still, holding that no general rule about pardon is laid down here, and that the whole clause is confined to a gross denial of God.

Gill takes the threat that follows as Joshua's jealousy over a people he knew to be prone to idolatry, set before them to make them cautious, and Wesley glosses the turning as goodness abused becoming fury. When they answer regardless, Clarke observes that they plainly understood no impossibility to lie on their side, and adds that had they sought God's gracious assistance in earnest they would have stood. Ellicott is drier, that once brought to the point no other answer was possible, since if Jehovah and the idols could not both be kept the idols had to go first. Keil and Delitzsch read Joshua's rejoinder as a legal one, that their own testimony will condemn them, and Clarke sharpens it into a formula, that conscience will be at once witness, judge and executioner.

Calvin sees here the point of the whole exchange, that Joshua never meant to terrify them away but to make the obligation more sacred by having them choose it themselves, and he notes with hindsight from Judges how quickly the promise faded once the older generation died. The command to put away the strange gods divides the sources over whether real images were still held, and Keil and Delitzsch prefer to read the phrase as within you, of idols of the heart. Calvin inclines the same way, thinking it improbable that after Achan's execution anyone dared keep Chaldean or Egyptian images in his house, though Wesley takes the opposite view and supposes some were kept either for the value of the material or from a secret hankering. Clarke presses for immediate action, since a promise loses its hold on the conscience unless performance begins at once, and Ellicott observes that no performance is recorded at all, no images buried or burned as in the days of Jacob or David, but only a verbal promise.
25:
Clarke notes that the Hebrew says Joshua cut the covenant, and takes the idiom to allude to a sacrifice offered on the occasion. Ellicott defines its content narrowly, a covenant that idolatry should not be tolerated in Israel, and sets it beside the later covenants of Asa, of Jehoiada under Joash, and of Josiah. Calvin insists that the statute and ordinance which follow are not some further speech of Joshua's, as some expositors have made them, but the law of Moses itself, since the whole transaction added no new heads but confirmed the doctrine they had already professed. Keil and Delitzsch describe the day in the same terms, as a solemn renewal of the covenant at Sinai after the pattern of Moses in the steppes of Moab, and Wesley adds that the statute bound their posterity as well as themselves.

On the writing, Clarke supposes Joshua used one of the blank columns of the great roll on which the law was written and which lay beside the ark. Ellicott makes far more of it, reading this as the second signature among the writers of the Old Testament after Moses and before Samuel, and inferring that those who followed Moses did not think of themselves as composing separate books but as adding their part to the book already begun. Calvin treats the volume as a public record deposited for perpetual remembrance, and observes that what is written often lies concealed in unopened books, which is why a second memorial was set where the eye could not miss it. Wesley reads it in the same practical way, that the record would stand as a witness for God against the people if he afterwards punished them, and thinks the agreement may itself have been cut into the stone as was then usual.

The oak stood by the sanctuary of the Lord, and here Keil and Delitzsch part from the others, refusing to let the phrase mean the ark brought over from the tabernacle for the ceremony. Calvin and Wesley take exactly that view, Calvin allowing that the ark had no perpetual station at Shechem but had been placed there so that the people might appear before God, and Wesley noting that a tree already standing was no breach of the law against planting a grove. That the stone had heard the words is figurative, and Wesley says so plainly, comparing the many places where hearing is ascribed to the heavens and the earth, while Clarke rests the image on the stone's permanence, which makes it as competent a witness as any man who had been present.

Calvin alone turns the memorial into a lament, granting that the divine word pierces even rocks so that deaf men find their condemnation echoed in the elements, and then asking who would not have supposed such a covenant secure for ages, when all Joshua's anxiety bought was a few years' obedience. Gill closes on the dismissal as Joshua's final leave of a people he would not outlive by long, and Clarke records that the Septuagint inserts a later verse of the chapter at this point.
29:
Keil and Delitzsch treat the renewal of the covenant as the end of Joshua's vocation, and explain that he never formally laid down his office because no successor had been appointed, the elders and the high priest with his Urim and Thummim being government enough. Clarke sets the death shortly after the assembly, his work done and his soul ripened, and notes that he reached exactly the age of Joseph. Ellicott reads the same figure the other way, that the mention of elders who outlived Joshua suggests his was a comparatively early death, and that had he laboured more for himself and less for Israel he might have lasted longer. Henry frames the whole ending with the observation that a book which began with triumphs closes with funerals, by which all the glory of man is stained.

Both Henry and Calvin fasten on the title given him after his death. Henry notes it is the same the text gave Moses at his end, and that though Joshua was in many respects the lesser man he was equal in this, since the servant who traded with two talents heard the same commendation as the one who traded with five. Calvin turns it against the survivors, arguing that so honourable a title left no excuse to men who shortly afterwards spurned the God who had worked wonders among them. He finds a tacit antithesis in the very statement that Israel served the Lord while Joshua lived, since to date their fidelity is to date its end.

Gill explains the burial in a field of his own estate by the custom of not burying within towns, and reports the addition of the Greek version that the stone knives of the circumcision at Gilgal were laid in the tomb, which he and an Arabic writer alike leave without foundation. Clarke gives the same addition more sympathetically, noting that Augustine quotes it in his questions on this book, and finds it very strange that no public mourning is recorded, guessing that Joshua had forbidden funeral pomp and was privately interred. Henry gathers a Jewish tradition about the hill of Gaash, that it trembled at the burial to upbraid Israel for not lamenting him as they ought, and compares the earthquake at the death of Christ. He also passes on Bishop Patrick's remark that no days of mourning were kept as they had been for Moses and Aaron, with the reason some of the fathers gave, that under the law men had cause to weep for the dead where the gospel gives cause to rejoice.

Keil and Delitzsch record simply that Joshua's labours did not remain without effect, since Israel served the Lord throughout his life and the lives of the elders who had seen what God did. Clarke qualifies this with the distinction he has drawn all along, that private idolatry persisted while public idolatry did not, and cites Calmet for a period of about fifteen years. Ellicott compares the whole episode to a primitive Church in Canaan, whose brief duration he finds matched by the primitive Church of the Roman Empire. Calvin generalises it into a law of church history, that gifted men preserve order while they live and that hidden impiety breaks out with unbridled licence once they are gone, which is also Henry's point when he remarks how much one head can hold up.
32:
Wesley recalls that Joseph had died in Egypt two hundred years before and had charged that his bones should not rest in a grave until Israel rested in the land of promise. Clarke thinks the burial was carried out once the conquest was complete and each tribe had received its inheritance, rather than being deferred until after Joshua's death, and Calvin infers the same from the fact that they waited for a peaceful habitation at Shechem. Gill notes that the carrying up of the bones is credited to Moses in one place and to the people in another, since it was done under his direction and their hands. Wesley draws the most from the coincidence, suggesting that one reason Joshua summoned all Israel to Shechem was to attend Joseph's coffin to the grave, so that the address in this chapter served as both a funeral sermon and a farewell, and that a man of exactly his ancestor's age might well have been reminded of his own end.

Calvin alone weighs the choice of the place, allowing that Joseph had designated no particular sepulchre and that laying him in the field Jacob had bought was a mark of respect. He adds a harder reading beside it, that the notice may be a censure on the people's sluggishness, since Joseph could not be laid with Abraham while that ground remained in enemy hands. He observes that Stephen speaks of the bones of the twelve patriarchs, thinks it not impossible that the other tribes gathered their forefathers' ashes out of emulation, and judges that a name has been confused in that passage where the field is said to have been bought by Abraham. He closes the whole commentary on the general point that Scripture dwells so often on burial because it is a symbol of the resurrection to come.

On Eleazar the sources agree only that he died about the time Joshua did, Clarke noting that some allow him six years more, and Wesley comparing the pairing to Aaron dying in the same year as Moses. Gill preserves the account in the Samaritan Chronicle that Eleazar made an end like Joshua's, gathering the chief men, charging them to obedience, taking his leave, and then stripping off the holy garments to clothe Phinehas with them. Ellicott calls Eleazar and Joshua the Moses and Aaron of their period and thinks it fitting that the book should end with the death of the counsellor at whose word Joshua was to go out and come in, while remarking that nothing but the official is recorded of him and not a word he spoke survives. The hill in Ephraim draws the same explanation from Ellicott and Wesley, that a priest's inheritance lay elsewhere and this was a special grant, convenient for attendance on the ark at Shiloh, though Clarke prefers to read it as a national acknowledgment of the zeal of Phinehas.

Clarke reports the long Septuagint addition here, which carries the story on to Phinehas succeeding his father, the people scattering to their cities, and Israel worshipping Astarte until they were given into the hand of Eglon for eighteen years. He then argues plainly that the last verses cannot be Joshua's, since no man records his own burial, and defends the practice by analogy with the continuations of Caesar, of Homer and of Virgil, none of which has ever thrown doubt on the authentic part. Ellicott is bleaker about what followed, that even zealous Phinehas lived to see Benjamin nearly exterminated for repeating the sin of the Canaanites, and that with Eleazar and Joshua the spirit of strict obedience largely passed away. Wesley ends on the same fact turned to comfort, that religion was kept up while Joshua lived and swiftly decayed once his generation was gone, which is why it is well for the church that Christ its Joshua remains with it always.
